problemText: Which of the following best defines what an organizational pattern is in an informational text?
choices: A series of interesting words that signal what the author thinks about the topic.
The shape a whole text uses to connect its paragraphs and ideas to one another.
The order in which sentences appear on the page from top to bottom.
A single sentence that tells the reader what the text will be about.
hints: An organizational pattern is not just about one sentence or one idea — it is about how the whole text holds together.
Think about how paragraphs connect to each other, not how individual words sound.

problemText:
Read this short text. Which organizational pattern does it use?

Paragraph 1: Honeybees collect pollen from flowers and bring it back to the hive. Paragraph 2: The bees store the pollen and mix it with nectar to make food for the colony. Paragraph 3: This stored food feeds the young bees and helps the colony survive the winter.
choices: Compare/contrast, because it describes bees at different stages of growth.
Chronological, because it lists what happens first, second, and third.
Cause/effect, because each step causes the next one to happen in the food-making chain.
Problem/solution, because the text explains how bees solve the problem of feeding the colony.
hints: Notice the signal words that connect the ideas — do they show time order, or do they show one action causing another?
Ask yourself: is this text explaining steps that follow each other in time, or is it explaining why each step leads to the next one?

problemText:
A student read this text and said it was organized in chronological order. Is the student correct? Explain your reasoning.

Paragraph 1: Glaciers are large, slow-moving rivers of ice. Paragraph 2: When glaciers move across the land, they carve deep valleys into the bedrock below because their weight and friction grind away rock over thousands of years. Paragraph 3: As a result of this grinding, many of the valleys we see in mountainous regions today were shaped by glaciers that melted away long ago.
choices: Yes, the student is correct, because the text moves through events that happened a long time ago.
Yes, the student is correct, because the three paragraphs appear in order from first to last.
No, the student is incorrect, because the text shows how one thing causes another to happen, not just events in time order.
No, the student is incorrect, because the text talks about the same subject twice and compares it to itself.
hints: Look at the signal words: 'because,' 'as a result' — what do they tell you about how the ideas connect?
Remember the trap from the lesson: just because events happen over time does not mean the text is organized chronologically.

problemText:
Read this text, then choose the best statement about its organizational pattern and why that pattern fits the topic.

Paragraph 1: Many students struggle to finish their homework because they feel overwhelmed by the amount of work. Paragraph 2: When students feel this way, they often procrastinate, which means they delay starting the work, and the deadline gets closer without any progress. Paragraph 3: One way students have solved this is by breaking homework into smaller chunks and completing one chunk at a time. Paragraph 4: As a result of this strategy, students report that they feel less anxious and finish their work on time more often.
choices: The text uses problem/solution because it names the struggle students face with homework and then explains a strategy that helps them solve it, which fits a topic about fixing a real trouble.

The text uses chronological order because it describes the homework process in the sequence a student follows, moving from starting the task, to getting distracted, to finally completing all the work step by step.
The text uses cause/effect because it identifies that overwhelm and procrastination cause missed deadlines and incomplete work, showing how one problem leads directly to another negative outcome.
The text uses compare/contrast because it examines the differences between how students felt before using the chunking strategy and how they feel after trying this new approach.
hints: Identify the real trouble first, then ask whether the text explains what fixed it.
Remember that a pattern must fit the topic — ask yourself what the text is really trying to do: explain why something happens, or explain how to fix something broken?

problemText:
A student said this text uses compare/contrast because it talks about how a butterfly is different from how it was before. Is this reasoning correct? Why or why not?

Paragraph 1: A caterpillar eats leaves and grows bigger, but it cannot fly. Paragraph 2: One day, the caterpillar stops eating and forms a hard shell called a chrysalis around itself. Paragraph 3: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body completely changes over several weeks, which causes it to transform into a butterfly with wings and a long tongue for sipping nectar. Paragraph 4: Once the butterfly emerges, it can fly away and search for flowers.
choices: Yes, the reasoning is correct, because any text that shows a before-and-after is organized as compare/contrast, and this text clearly describes what the creature was like before and what it became after the transformation.

No, the reasoning is wrong because the text actually uses chronological order to show the stages of one creature's life cycle from the beginning to the end, and life cycles need time order to make sense.

No, the reasoning is wrong because a before-and-after of a single subject showing stages of development over time follows cause and effect, where each stage causes the next one to happen, not a side-by-side comparison of two different things.
Yes, the reasoning is correct, because the text mentions both caterpillars and butterflies, which are two separate living things being examined and compared to each other throughout the paragraphs.
hints: Ask yourself: does this text introduce two separate things to set side by side, or does it follow one creature through its life stages in order?
Remember the trap from the lesson: before-and-after does not automatically mean compare/contrast — it could be chronological if it is showing stages of a life cycle.

problemText:
Read this text and then choose the correct pattern and explanation. Pay close attention to whether the pattern truly fits the topic the text is explaining.

Paragraph 1: Many forests in North America were cut down in the 1800s, so animals that lived there lost their homes and had nowhere to find food. Paragraph 2: Because of this loss of habitat, some animal populations shrank dangerously, which caused species like the eagle and the wolf to almost disappear forever. Paragraph 3: Starting in the 1900s, the government created national forests and protected areas to give animals safe places to live again. Paragraph 4: As a result of these protected areas, eagle and wolf populations recovered over the next hundred years.
choices: Cause/effect, because the text explains how cutting down forests caused animal populations to shrink, even though it also mentions a solution.

Problem/solution, because the text first names the real trouble of habitat loss and shrinking animal populations, then explains how the government's protected areas fixed the problem, which fits a topic about solving a real conservation challenge.
Chronological, because the text moves through events from the 1800s, to the 1900s, to modern times in time order.
Compare/contrast, because the text shows the difference between forests that were cut down and forests that were protected.
hints: Notice that the text contains cause/effect signal words, but ask yourself: is the main job of the text to explain cause and effect throughout, or is it to name a problem and explain a fix?
Remember: naming the pattern is only half the job — you also need to explain whether it truly fits what the topic is trying to do.

problemText: What is the difference between an author's purpose and an author's topic? Explain what each one means.
choices: The topic is how long the text is, and the purpose is how many readers it reaches.
The purpose is the subject the author writes about, and the topic is why the author wrote the text.
The topic is the subject the author writes about, and the purpose is the reason the author wrote the text.
The purpose and topic are the same thing, just two different words for the idea the author is discussing.
hints: Think about the worked example with the cafeteria announcements. Both versions had the same topic. What was different?
Purpose answers 'why did the author write this?' Topic answers 'what is this text about?'

problemText: Read this sentence from a school announcement: 'The library is extending its hours to 5 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays starting next week.' Which purpose does this sentence most clearly signal, and why?
choices: Persuade, because it tells readers the library is a good place to study.
Persuade, because it asks readers to use the library more often.
Inform, because it explains when something will happen without asking readers to feel or do anything.
Inform, because it uses the word 'starting,' which is a neutral word.
hints: Look for judgment words or calls to action in the sentence. Do you see any?
The sentence reports a schedule. Does reporting a schedule count as neutral word choice, or is it trying to persuade the reader?

problemText: Read this sentence from a school newsletter: 'Every parent should insist that the district hire more counselors because students deserve better access to mental health support.' Which element of this sentence most clearly reveals the author's purpose to persuade?
choices: The word 'should' gives a command and tells the reader what to do or believe.
The phrase 'school newsletter' shows this is official writing.
The mention of counselors tells the reader what the text is about.
The length of the sentence shows it is trying to persuade rather than inform.
hints: Look at the types of words the lesson calls 'judgment words' or words that ask readers to act. Which one is in this sentence?
A sentence that tells someone what they 'should' do is giving a command. Commands are a type of persuasive language.

problemText: A passage about a new school dress code includes only examples of problems caused by loose, colorful clothing. It then ends with 'Students will focus better on learning when they wear the standard uniform.' Which two features work together to show the author's purpose is to persuade readers that the dress code is necessary?
choices: The passage selects only examples that support uniforms and uses the word 'better' to describe the outcome, creating a one-sided argument that appeals to readers' desire for student success.
The passage selects only examples that favor the dress code, and the closing sentence makes a judgment about what will help students learn.
The passage includes specific details about clothing problems and repeats the word 'uniform' multiple times throughout to reinforce the main message about dress code requirements.
The passage presents evidence about how dress codes affect behavior and uses persuasive language to convince readers that uniforms are the only solution to school distractions.
hints: The lesson says selected details reveal purpose just as much as word choice does. Look for which choice names both a detail choice AND a word choice together.
Remember the worked example about the phone ban. It selected only examples favoring one side and ended with a judgment. What two things made that persuasive?

problemText: Two passages describe the same community garden project. Passage X reports that 'thirty neighbors planted vegetables, five neighbors donated tools, and two neighbors left before finishing.' Passage Y states that 'the community came together to create a garden, and it proves that when people work as one, amazing things happen.' Which statement correctly identifies both authors' purposes and points to proof from the lesson?
choices: Both passages persuade because they both talk about the community garden and its success.
Passage X informs by reporting outcomes on more than one side, while Passage Y persuades by including only positive details and a judgment about what the project 'proves.'
Passage X persuades because it mentions the number of neighbors, while Passage Y informs because it uses the word 'amazing.'
Passage X informs about the garden, and Passage Y informs about community, so both passages have different purposes even though they cover the same topic.
hints: Look at what details each passage chose to include. Does one side with only good news, or does one report both positive and negative outcomes?
The lesson says an informing passage about an event 'would usually report outcomes on more than one side.' Which passage does that?

problemText: Read this announcement about a new after-school club: 'The Art Club meets every Tuesday and Thursday from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. in the art room. All supplies are provided by the school at no cost to students. Students with any level of art experience are welcome, and the club's only requirement is that members stay for the entire meeting.' If the author's purpose were to persuade students to join the club, which sentence would need to be added or changed, and why?
choices: A sentence stating when the club was created, because readers need to know the club's history.
A sentence explaining where the art room is located, because readers need to understand why the location matters.

A sentence saying something like 'You should join because art club gives you a place to grow as an artist and meet new friends,' because the announcement currently has no judgment words or call to action.
A sentence adding that some students have won art awards through the club, because all persuasive texts need to include examples of success.
hints: The announcement currently uses neutral language: it explains the schedule, cost, and requirements without judging or commanding. What would change that?
The lesson says persuasive language includes judgment words or calls to action. Look at which choice adds the kind of language the lesson identifies as persuasive.

problemText: A claim counts as SUPPORTED when a reason and evidence are attached to it. Which of the following best describes what this means?
choices: The claim uses confident words like 'clearly' or 'obviously' so readers will believe it and accept the statement without needing proof.
The claim repeats the same idea in multiple sentences throughout the text to reinforce the message and make it stick in the reader's mind.
The claim sounds like something most people in the school already know and agree with, so it feels familiar and commonly accepted.
The claim has a sentence nearby that explains why it should be believed and includes a specific fact or example to back that up.
hints: Look for the definition of 'supported' in the lesson — what two things must be present?
Remember: evidence is a fact or example, not just a feeling or a confident tone.

problemText: Read this passage from an argument about adding more lunch periods to the school day. Then identify which specific claim is NOT SUPPORTED by any reason or evidence. "Lincoln Middle School should add a lunch period before noon instead of at 12:30 pm. Students eat lunch too late in the day right now. When students eat late, they get hungry again before the end of the school day, and that makes it harder for them to focus on afternoon lessons. Late lunch is also super unfair."
choices: Late lunch is also super unfair.
Students eat lunch too late in the day right now.
When students eat late, they get hungry again before the end of the school day.
Lincoln Middle School should add a lunch period before noon instead of at 12:30 pm.
hints: Follow the two steps: find the claim sentence, then read the sentence or two right around it. Is there a reason and a fact?
Notice which sentence has no explanation following it — the argument simply moves on.

problemText: Read this argument about adding a water fountain in the gymnasium. "The gym needs its own water fountain because students get very thirsty during basketball practice. During a forty-minute practice, students sweat a lot and lose water from their bodies, so they need to drink more than usual. Right now students have to leave the gym to find a water fountain down the hall, which wastes practice time." Which specific claim is SUPPORTED by a reason and evidence?
choices: Students get very thirsty during basketball practice because they sweat a lot during a forty-minute practice and lose water from their bodies.
The gym needs its own water fountain so that students do not have to leave practice and waste time walking down the hall.
Students have to leave the gym during practice.
Water fountains are the most important part of any school building.
hints: Find each specific claim and check the next sentence — is there a reason and a fact that backs it up?
The correct answer is a claim that the text actually explains or gives a concrete problem for.

problemText: Read this argument about starting a school garden. "Meadows Middle School should start a vegetable garden in the south courtyard. The garden would teach students where their food comes from because they would plant seeds, water the plants, and watch them grow from start to finish. Growing vegetables also teaches students science because they learn about soil, sunlight, and how plants use water and nutrients to grow." One of these specific claims sounds well-backed at first, but when you check carefully for a reason and evidence, you find it is actually NOT SUPPORTED. Which one is it?
choices: Growing vegetables teaches science because students learn about soil and sunlight.
The garden would teach students where food comes from.
Students would plant seeds, water the plants, and watch them grow.
A garden in the south courtyard would be useful to have.
hints: Watch out: a sentence that describes what would happen is not the same as a claim that is backed up by a reason and evidence.
Ask yourself: which sentence tells what students would do, but does not explain why the garden should be built?

problemText: Read this passage and answer the question that follows. "The school should start a breakfast club that meets every Tuesday. Students who eat breakfast do better in school because their brains work better when they have fuel in the morning. Eating breakfast within one hour of waking up helps students focus, remember information, and stay awake during class. A breakfast club would also be the best way to make the school better." Which statement correctly sorts one of the specific claims as SUPPORTED or NOT SUPPORTED and gives the right reason?
choices: The claim about students doing better in school is NOT SUPPORTED because the text does not say what time breakfast club would meet.

The claim that students do better in school when they eat breakfast is SUPPORTED because the text explains that eating breakfast helps their brains work better and gives examples of how it helps them focus and remember.
The claim about focusing and remembering is NOT SUPPORTED because it comes before the claim about breakfast club.
The claim that breakfast club would be the best way to make the school better is NOT SUPPORTED because no reason or evidence is given for why this is true.
hints: Check each claim and the sentence or two right around it — does a reason and a fact follow, or does the text simply move on?
Remember: 'best' is a confident word, but confident words are not evidence. Look for an actual reason and fact.

problemText: Read this argument. "Central Middle School should extend recess by ten minutes. Students need more outdoor time to be healthy and happy. Medical experts say that children should get at least sixty minutes of physical activity every day, and most students at Central only get thirty minutes during the school day, which means they have to make up the rest after school. However, the claim that 'Recess is the most fun part of the day' appears at the very end of the passage and is immediately followed by a period." Based on the lesson, explain why the second claim (about recess being the most fun) is NOT SUPPORTED, and identify what common mistake might lead someone to think it was.
choices: The claim about recess being fun is not supported because no reason or evidence follows it, even though it appears at the end where a strong finish is expected. A careless reader might assume such a statement must be backed up just because of where it is placed.
The claim about recess being fun is not supported because it is an opinion about feelings rather than a factual statement, and opinions cannot ever be supported by any kind of evidence or reasoning.

The claim about recess being fun is not supported because it uses the word 'most' instead of providing a specific measurement or comparison that would make the statement clearer and more believable to the reader.
The claim about recess being fun is not supported because it refers to a personal experience or preference rather than establishing a connection to the main argument about extending recess time.
hints: Remember the lesson: do not grade the claim as good or bad, just check whether a reason and evidence are there. Position matters — unsupported claims can hide where they should be strong.
A claim at the end of the passage does not automatically count as supported, even though it is a prominent position. You must still follow the two steps.

problemText: You are comparing two accounts of the same school event. Before you look for what is different between them, what must you check first?
choices: That both accounts describe the same real event on the same day and place
That one account is longer than the other one, since longer accounts tend to be more reliable and detailed
That both accounts use identical words and sentences throughout, proving they are copies of the same original source
That both accounts agree perfectly on every single detail without any differences or disagreements at all
hints: The lesson calls this step 'confirming the event matches' before comparing anything else.
You need to verify the foundation—the same day, place, and happening—before moving forward.

problemText: Read these two accounts of a field trip. Source A says the bus left at 8:15 a.m. and arrived at the museum at 9:00 a.m. Source B says the bus left at 8:15 a.m. and the students spent two hours looking at dinosaur fossils. Do these two accounts contradict each other?
choices: Yes, because Source A mentions the time and Source B does not
No, because both facts can be true of the same field trip without clashing
Yes, because one account talks about arrival time and the other talks about activities
No, but Source A is more complete than Source B
hints: The lesson teaches that different details do not make accounts wrong—only facts that actually clash count as disagreement.
Ask yourself: can a bus leave at 8:15, arrive at 9:00, AND the students spend two hours looking at fossils all on the same day?

problemText: Two accounts describe the same morning soccer game. Source A focuses on how nervous the goalkeeper felt before the game started and how proud she was after her team won. Source B focuses on the final score, the number of goals each player made, and the weather conditions. Which statement best explains the difference between these two accounts?
choices: Source A is more truthful because it explores the goalkeeper's inner feelings and emotional reactions to the game
Source B is more complete because it includes numerical data about goals and weather observations from the game
The accounts emphasize different details because the writers chose to focus on different parts of the same game
The accounts contradict each other because they do not say the same thing about the soccer game
hints: The lesson calls this difference 'emphasis' and 'selection'—writers choose what to focus on and what to leave out.
Remember: choosing different details to include is not the same as disagreement or one account being wrong.

problemText: Two accounts describe a library book donation. Source A is a warm thank-you note from a library volunteer: 'We had such wonderful community members come by on Saturday with boxes and bags of books. The children's section received so many new stories, and it was heartwarming to see families bringing books together.' Source B is the library's official report: 'On Saturday, the library received a book donation. A total of 347 books were added to the collection: 180 to the children's section, 95 to young adult, and 72 to adult fiction.' Both accounts are about the same donation on the same Saturday. Which of the following is a fact that BOTH accounts share, and which details belong to only one account each?
choices: Shared fact: families brought books. Source A adds the exact book count; Source B adds that it was heartwarming.
Shared fact: a book donation happened on Saturday at the library. Source A adds warm feeling and community spirit; Source B adds the exact number of books and how they were sorted.
Shared fact: 347 books were donated. Source A adds nothing; Source B adds the breakdown by section.
Shared fact: the children's section received new books. Source A adds that families worked together; Source B adds that it was officially recorded.
hints: Start by finding what both accounts actually state in common—the base event that both could not leave out.
Then list what is unique to each: Source A's emphasis on feelings and warmth, and Source B's numbers and organization.

problemText: Two students wrote accounts of a school talent show. Maya's account (a personal email to her grandma) says: 'The talent show on Friday night was so much fun! My best friend sang a solo, and I could tell she was nervous at first, but by the middle of her song she was beaming. I was on the edge of my seat the whole time.' The school's official program says: 'The Spring Talent Show was held Friday evening in the auditorium. Fifteen students performed, including singing, dancing, comedy, and instrumental acts. The event lasted 90 minutes and raised $200 for the school arts program.' After you confirm both accounts describe the same event, what can you conclude about why the two accounts are so different from each other?
choices: Maya's account is incomplete and therefore less useful than the school program because it does not include facts like the number of performers or how much money was raised
The accounts differ in stance and emphasis because Maya wrote from a personal, feeling-focused viewpoint while the program reported facts and numbers that were its job to record
One account must be wrong because they do not contain the same information
Maya's account is better because it captures the real experience while the program is too dry and formal
hints: The lesson teaches that stance is the attitude or feeling behind the words—a personal letter sounds warm, while an official report sounds plain and factual.
Think about what each writer's job was: Maya was writing to family about her experience, while the program needed to record attendance, format, and fundraising results.

problemText: Two accounts describe a community cleanup day. Source A (a volunteer's blog post) says: 'On the chilly Saturday morning of March 10th, our neighborhood cleanup crew met at Riverside Park. Working together made the morning fly by, and seeing the park transform from littered paths to clean open spaces gave everyone such a sense of accomplishment. By the end, we were all smiling despite our tired muscles.' Source B (the city parks department report) says: 'On March 10th, volunteer crews completed a cleanup of Riverside Park. In four hours, the crew removed 340 pounds of litter from trails and picnic areas, cleared five blocked storm drains, and filled the park's recycling bins. Weather conditions were cool and clear. The cleanup will extend the park's maintenance cycle by approximately two weeks.' You have confirmed both accounts describe the same cleanup on the same day at the same park. Now identify: (1) one fact that BOTH sources state, (2) one detail that appears only in Source A and explains what it shows about the volunteer's stance, and (3) one detail that appears only in Source B and what it shows about the writer's purpose.
choices: Both state: the park was cleaned on March 10th. Source A only: tired muscles—shows volunteers focused on the effort. Source B only: removed 340 pounds—shows the writer was counting results.

Both state: a community cleanup happened at Riverside Park on Saturday, March 10th, in cool weather. Source A only: people smiled and felt accomplished—shows the volunteer wrote from a personal, feeling-focused stance. Source B only: removed 340 pounds and cleared storm drains—shows the writer was recording specific work done and its impact on maintenance.
Both state: the park was cleaned. Source A only: morning flew by—shows volunteers were distracted. Source B only: four hours of work—shows the city pays volunteers by the hour.
Both state: the crew was tired after the work. Source A only: the paths looked better—shows volunteers were optimistic. Source B only: cool and clear weather—shows the city controls the weather.
hints: First, find the shared fact that appears in both accounts without adding opinion or feeling.

Then separate: what emotion or personal detail did Source A add (that shows its warm, personal stance), and what measurement or work-tracking detail did Source B add (that shows its role as an official report)?
